column2: An independent quantitative check
column3: An accounting proposed by the same people who then use it to argue for a configuration invites one obvious objection: that the charges were chosen because a particular aircraft happens not to pay them.

column2: An independent quantitative check
column3: The objection arises at the title, not at the ledger, so it is answered here — before any configuration is described — and it is answered in the only way that settles anything, by testing a prediction the accounting makes against numbers this work did not produce.

column2: An independent quantitative check
column3: **What follows is not a test of the whole framework.** It checks one falsifiable consequence on one independent data set.

column2: An independent quantitative check
column3: That is a narrow thing, and it is stated narrowly.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: **The prediction has two halves, and only the first is a derivation.** Saying so is what makes the check worth running.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: **First half, derived from Section 2.** A configuration carrying a dedicated lift system pays for it in gross weight, and the payment is amplified: additional empty mass enters through a multiplier that grows as the empty-mass fraction rises, and the same increment is charged again in hover.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: **Second half, not derived.** That the cruise efficiency the arrangement buys does not cover that payment.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: Section 2 predicts the charge and the amplification; **it does not prove that the credit must lose.** A dedicated lift system raises the empty-mass fraction and may lower the energy fraction at the same time, and which wins is a closure result rather than a consequence of the accounting.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: The check tests the second half on independent data, with the first half supplying the reason to expect the outcome: the weight charge is amplified by a multiplier, while the efficiency credit enters linearly through the cruise lift-to-drag ratio.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: That distinction decides what a failure would mean.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: **If some data set showed the credit covering the charge, Bill 1 would not be refuted** — the mass would still have been paid.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: What would be refuted is the expectation that the amplified charge outweighs the linear credit, and that is worth testing precisely because it could go either way.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: **The prediction is also mission-dependent**, and the page would be weaker for hiding it.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: The mass charge of carried lift hardware is roughly fixed; the efficiency credit accumulates with distance.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: A long enough mission is where the credit is most likely to cover the charge, and the mission used below is short.

column2: The prediction, stated before the data
column3: **The counter-set is therefore a common-mission sizing study at longer range in which a dedicated-lift configuration is both more efficient and no heavier than one without.** None is known to the authors, and the invitation is meant literally.

column2: The data
column3: The check uses a NASA study that sizes **five VTOL architecture families**, most in two propulsion variants — nine designs in all — against a single mission with common tools and common assumptions.

column2: The data
column3: It was conducted for its own purposes, has no relationship to the present work, and does not use the three-bill accounting of Section 2 or any framework derived from it.

column2: The data
column3: It is used here for three reasons, stated so that the choice is not merely the one that agreed: it holds the mission fixed across architecture families, it applies one set of tools to all of them, and it reports both quantities this prediction needs.

column2: The data
column3: The mission is 1 200 lb of payload over 75 nautical miles.

column2: The data
column3: Three of the nine designs matter here.

column2: The data
column3: The turboshaft quadrotor reaches an effective lift-to-drag ratio of 4.9 at a design gross weight of 3 678 lb, with no dedicated lift group: its rotors serve both regimes.

column2: The data
column3: **The turbo-electric lift-plus-cruise design reaches 8.5 at 7 271 lb and carries a dedicated lift group — eight lift motors beside its cruise motor.

column2: The data
column3: The turbo-electric tilt-wing reaches 8.6 at 6 584 lb with none: eight proprotors, reoriented.**

column2: The result
column3: **The primary comparison is the last two designs**, because they isolate the charge.

column2: The result
column3: The lift-plus-cruise and tilt-wing entries share the mission, the payload, the turbo-electric propulsion architecture and the presence of a cruising wing.

column2: The result
column3: **They are not identical in every other respect** — one stops its lift rotors in the airstream and drives a separate pusher, the other reorients its proprotors on a tilting wing — **but the difference the comparison turns on is that one carries a dedicated lift group through cruise and the other does not.** The comparison is the closest the published set comes to isolating that charge; it is not a controlled experiment.

column2: The result
column3: **The tilt-wing is 1.2 % better in effective cruise efficiency and 9.4 % lighter.** The dedicated lift group buys no cruise-efficiency advantage at all here — it is marginally behind — and the design gross weights differ by 687 lb in the tilt-wing's favour.

column2: The result
column3: **That figure is the net difference between two architectures, not the measured mass of a lift group**, and the published weight breakdown is what makes it informative rather than merely large.

column2: The result
column3: **The published weight breakdown shows the transfer property of Section 2 — the mechanism giving part of the structural saving back — inside a breakdown this work did not produce**, although the categories it reports do not account for the whole difference (Supplement S4).

column2: The result
column3: **And the source states the second half of the prediction in its own words.** Discussing why the all-electric lift-plus-cruise design is the heaviest in the set, the study writes that the high cruise efficiency of the lift-plus-cruise type reduces battery weight compared with the quadrotor, *"but not enough to counter the increase in structure and propulsion weight."* That is the efficiency credit conceded and found insufficient, by the authors of the data rather than by the authors of the prediction.

column2: The result
column3: **The quadrotor is reported for scale, and the isolation test above is what carries the prediction**: against it the lift-plus-cruise design changes three things at once, and the contrast is in Supplement S4.

column2: The result
column3: **The framework does not predict any of these numbers**; without the input fractions it predicts no magnitudes.

column2: The result
column3: What it predicts is that the amplified weight charge survives the efficiency credit, and on the isolated pair it does so with the credit reduced to nothing.

column2: The tilt-wing is the instructive case
column3: The tilt-wing is the entry that carries the isolation test above, and it is also the entry that denies this paper a claim it might otherwise be read as making.

column2: The tilt-wing is the instructive case
column3: **The architecture proposed later in this paper is not the only way to avoid the first charge.** The tilting family avoids it too — it carries no dedicated lift group, it is the lighter of the two matched designs, and an independent set says so.

column2: The tilt-wing is the instructive case
column3: The margin in cruise efficiency is one tenth and nothing is claimed from its direction; what matters is that the dedicated lift group does not buy an efficiency advantage to set against its mass.

column2: The tilt-wing is the instructive case
column3: **Second, and this is what the entry is actually for: the tilt-wing is the transfer property of Section 2 appearing in someone else's data.** It does not escape the accounting by avoiding the mass charge; it *moves* the charge — to the mechanism that reorients its propulsors, with the actuation, the gyroscopic coupling and the transition control problem that Section 2 assigns to that family.

column2: The tilt-wing is the instructive case
column3: The entry therefore does two jobs: it denies this paper a uniqueness it has not earned, and it confirms the property the accounting is built on.

column2: The tilt-wing is the instructive case
column3: What separates the tilting family from the configuration described later is not this axis; it is what each pays, and a sizing study does not settle that.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: It establishes that one prediction of the accounting holds on data produced elsewhere, for purposes unrelated to this argument.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: That is the whole of it.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: **It does not establish that the accounting is complete**, that the three charges are the only costs an architecture pays, or that avoiding them makes an aircraft better.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: The accounting says an architecture that avoids the three is cheaper in those three currencies and nothing more; a configuration may avoid all three and still be unbuildable, uncontrollable, or unsuited to its mission.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: Sections 10 and 14 are about exactly that possibility for the configuration proposed here.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: **It does not establish anything about the configuration this paper proposes**, which has not yet been described, and which is not in the study used here.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: A reader who wants to know whether the accounting flatters that configuration will have to wait for Section 11, where it is applied to it and where the answer is not uniformly favourable.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: What the check is for is narrower and comes earlier:

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: **an instrument whose first use is to measure the thing its authors are advocating should be shown working on something else first.** That is what this section does, and it is the reason it appears here rather than after the aircraft.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: **The instrument is now fixed, and it is not modified again.** Sections 2 and 3 defined what any architecture in this corner pays and what escaping it would require; this section tested one falsifiable consequence of that definition on data produced by other people for other aircraft.

column2: What this check does and does not establish
column3: **Everything that follows is measured with it rather than added to it.** The next two sections describe the two capabilities the mission asks for, one at a time and each against the family that structurally lacks it, before Section 7 asks whether one aircraft can hold both.
